title: Slot-based Burst Scheduler and Latency Fences — PRD proposal
body:
Purpose:
This doc proposes a slot-based burst scheduling model paired with "latency fences" for Dedicated capacity. Goal is to give tenants predictable latency under bursty demand while enabling controlled, opportunistic bursts and graceful degradation for lower-priority workloads.

Problem statement:
- Tenants experience highly variable latency during microburst windows: tail latency spikes for latency-sensitive routes while batchy/cheap workloads soak GPU capacity.
- Existing heuristics (credit pools, simple burst credits) can lead to long tail latencies or over-aggressive preemption that disrupts throughput.
- We need an operator-friendly model that composes with Dedicated pool autoscaling and tenant isolation controls without manual, per-tenant tuning.

High-level approach:
- Introduce the concept of "slots": discrete runtime admission units representing a fraction of GPU concurrency. Slots are consumed by incoming requests and released when KV cache/beam search completes.
- Define tenant priority lanes (P0, P1, P2) mapped to slot reservation quotas and soft/ hard latency fences.
- Implement a latency fence mechanism: when P0 requests enter a fence, system enforces a target p95 latency by reserving minimal free slots or preempting opportunistic slots from P2 after a short grace window.
- Dynamic slot sizing: slots are re-sized based on observed seq-length distributions and model memory pressure so a slot is an adaptive concurrency token rather than a fixed thread.

Goals and success metrics:
- P0 p95 latency under microbursts: <= configured SLO (e.g., 120ms) for 99% of bursts in a 30-day window.
- Throughput retention: overall tokens/sec drop <= 15% compared to baseline without fences for bursty mixes.
- Cost efficiency: autoscaler can avoid >20% additional reserved capacity compared to naive overprovisioning while meeting latency targets.
- Operational tractability: rollout and debugging via Console charts and automated alerting (e.g., "fence-trips", preempt-count, slot-pressure).

Design details:
1) Slot model and lifecycle:
  - A pool of max_slots per node/gang is derived from GPU memory and kernel concurrency. Example: a V100 rack might have 128 slots at small-seq workloads; for long-seq requests slot-count shrinks to keep memory constraints.
  - Requests acquire 1 or more slots depending on predicted peak KV + beam footprint. For multi-turn chat, the runtime holds slots only for the active decode window and yields during user think-time if configured.
  - Slots have a lease TTL (default 2s) and can be greedily reused if the request finishes early.

2) Priority lanes and reserved quotas:
  - Each tenant can be assigned to a lane with a reserved_min_slots and reserved_max_burst.
  - P0: latency-critical (webhooks, sync calls) — guaranteed min slots, allowed short bursts up to reserved_max_burst.
  - P1: mixed (background interactive) — small guarantee, prioritized behind P0 for fence triggers.
  - P2: opportunistic (batch embeddings, offline rerank) — no minimum, eligible to be preempted or delayed.

3) Latency fences (runtime enforcement):
  - Fence trigger: when observed p95 latency for P0 exceeds threshold over a short rolling window (e.g., 30s), a fence enters enforcement state.
  - Enforcement actions, in order: 
      a) Activate soft-eviction: stop scheduling new P2 requests and throttle P1 concurrency.
      b) If pressure persists > fence_grace (default 3s), initiate slot reclaim protocols: mark opportunistic slots reclaimable and shift weight to ensure P0 gets reserved_min_slots.
      c) If still unresolved, escalate to preemption: pause lower-priority decodes mid-run if safe (checkpoint + resume), or reject with informative 429 + retry-after headers for non-critical requests.
  - Console exposes fence metrics: fence_count, average duration, preemptions, and tenant-visible "fence incidents" for CS/SE review.

4) Interaction with autoscaler and Dedicated pool capacity:
  - Autoscaler will consume slot pressure signals as an input channel: sustained slot saturation across nodes triggers scale up; transient fence events do NOT autoscale unless repeated over a threshold window (configurable).
  - Reserved capacity admission: when a customer purchases a reserved commitment, we convert that to floor reserved_min_slots across the pool with a higher fence priority and faster grace timeout.
  - Soft-burst credits are implemented by allowing a tenant to consume up to reserved_max_burst above reserved_min, charged at per-token premium or debited from burst-credit ledger.

5) Operational controls and UI/Console features:
  - Per-tenant panel showing: current slots in use, reserved_min, burst_spend (credit), recent fence events, predicted slot pressure heatmap.
  - Route-level knobs: route_priority (P0/P1/P2), detect_long_seq flag, fence_sensitivity slider for customers with special latency needs.
  - Alerts: "fence trip" (p95 breached), "preemptions rising" (>N preemptions/min), "burst credit exhausted".

6) Safety and degradation semantics:
  - Preemption is best-effort and only for preemptible workloads; default customer routes remain non-preemptible unless explicitly allowed.
  - Backoff semantics for retried requests to avoid stampeding: exponential backoff with jitter and server-supplied Retry-After when returning 429.
  - Cache warming and KV affinity: tenants with high P0 traffic get early KV-cache population hints to reduce slot duration on warm requests.

Implementation roadmap and phases:
- Phase 0 (spike, 4w): runtime feasibility spike — prototype slot token system in a single-node dev-runtime, measure slot granularity vs seq-length.
- Phase 1 (alpha, 8w): implement slot pool + simple lane admission, soft-eviction rules, Console readouts for a single Dedicated cluster. Limited to engineering tenants.
- Phase 2 (beta, 12w): add latency fences with grace windows, autoscaler integration, soft-burst ledger and billing hooks. Open to select customer pilots.
- Phase 3 (ga, 12w): wider rollout, preemption safeguards, tenant-facing UI, docs, runbooks, and SRE oncall playbooks.

Runbook excerpts (for SRE/ops):
- Detect: alert on "fence trip" with p95 and node slot_utilization > 85% over 30s.
- Mitigate: temporarily increase reserved_min_slots for affected P0 tenants (via emergency override) or shift lower-priority tenants to a spillover pool.
- Escalate: if >3 regions show sustained fences for >10m, initiate cross-region failover per Dedicated DR procedures.

Sample policy snippet (illustrative):
- tenant: acme-payments
  route_priority: P0
  reserved_min_slots: 16
  reserved_max_burst: 32
  fence_sensitivity: high
  preemptible: false

Open questions and risks:
- How to safely perform mid-decode preemption for large models without user-visible artifacts? Requires runtime checkpoints + QA on resumed sequences.
- Billing complexity: how granular should burst pricing be? Per-token premium vs time-windowed burst buckets?
- Predictive slot allocation: can we use ML to predict slot hold time to better schedule bursts? (Research spike needed)
- Multi-tenant fairness across heterogeneous instance types: fairness metrics must normalize for slot size differences.

Next steps:
- Run Phase 0 spike in staging with a synthetic mix (50% P2 embedding jobs, 40% P1 interactive, 10% P0 web calls) and collect baseline p95 and token throughput.
- Create JIRA epic and link to implementation PR.
- Draft Console UX mockups for lane controls and fence incident timelines and run a quick design review.

Appendix A — measurement plan:
- Baseline tests: microburst generator (100qps for 30s windows) across 1–3 concurrent tenants; measure p50/p95/p99 per-lane and slot utilization.
- Success gates prior to beta: P0 p95 under configured SLO across 95% of synthetic bursts; preemption artifacts rate < 0.1%.

Appendix B — related work / references:
- Credit-pool approach (existing docs) — pros/cons summary and why slot model helps with fine-grained admission.
- Research notes: checkpoint-based preemption drafts (Ravi P.) and backend scheduling sim (Liam O.).
